title: 06. Distributed Systems & Consistency: Distributed Systems Basics

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A distributed system is a collection of independent compute nodes that coordinate solely by passing messages over an unreliable network to appear as a single coherent service, while accepting that any node may fail independently, clocks may disagree, and the network may partition at any time.

A distributed system is what you get the moment one process cannot do the job alone and you start asking other machines — across a rack, a datacenter, or a continent — to help. The textbook definition (Tanenbaum and Van Steen) is blunt: it is a system in which components located on networked computers communicate and coordinate their actions only by passing messages. That single word — *only* — carries the entire difficulty of the field. If you cannot share memory, you cannot atomically read a flag another process set; if you cannot trust the network, you cannot tell the difference between a slow reply, a lost reply, and a crashed peer; if you cannot trust clocks, you cannot use timestamps to order events unambiguously. Everything else in distributed systems — replication, consensus, sharding, consistency models — is a reaction to those three facts.

The first law of the discipline is that **partial failure is the norm, not the exception**. In a single process, a crash takes the whole program down — clean, total, observable. In a distributed system, one node out of fifty may freeze while the other forty-nine keep serving traffic. Worse, the other forty-nine cannot immediately tell whether the frozen node is dead, slow, or partitioned away from them. Peter Deutsch's *Fallacies of Distributed Computing* — written in the Sun Microsystems era and still quoted by every SRE at Netflix and Uber — enumerates the assumptions beginners wrongly make: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, and transport cost is zero. Every one of those assumptions has caused a real production outage. Kafka brokers that silently drop messages when a NIC duplex-mismatches; Kubernetes controllers that fight because the API server is reachable from one network segment but not another; Redis Cluster re-shards that stall because a 100ms jitter tips over a 50ms timeout. The lesson is not that distributed systems are impossible — clearly Google, Amazon and Meta run them at planet scale — but that every design decision must price in the cost of these fallacies.

Real-world deployments illustrate the spectrum. **Google's MapReduce** is the canonical example of coordinated distributed batch processing: a master assigns map and reduce tasks to thousands of workers, restarts failed tasks idempotently, and writes output to GFS — itself a distributed file system that chunks files into 64MB blocks replicated across three nodes. **Apache Kafka clusters** run as a set of brokers that replicate partition logs across followers using an ISR (in-sync replicas) set; if a broker dies, the controller elects a new partition leader from the ISR in seconds, and producers choose between `acks=0`, `acks=1`, and `acks=all` to trade latency against durability. **The Kubernetes control plane** is a four-process distributed system (kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager) sitting on top of etcd, itself a Raft-replicated key-value store; every cluster-state change flows through the API server into etcd and is fanned out to watchers, with conflict resolution done via resource-version optimistic concurrency.

The CAP theorem (Gilbert-Lynch, 2002) frames the hard choice: during a network partition you must pick either Consistency (refuse stale reads) or Availability (serve them). PACELC (Abadi, 2010) extends this to *else* — when there is no partition, you still choose between Latency and Consistency. Spanner picks CP/EL: it pays TrueTime-driven commit waits to stay linearizable. Cassandra picks AP/EL: it accepts stale reads for single-digit-millisecond p99. Neither is wrong; each is the right answer for a different workload. Clock skew is the silent assassin. A 200ms NTP drift between a primary and a replica makes last-write-wins logic silently corrupt data; TrueTime in Spanner bounds uncertainty to under 7ms by using GPS and atomic clocks in every datacenter. Logical clocks (Lamport, vector clocks) sidestep the problem by tracking *happens-before* relationships instead of wall time.

The central trade-off is simplicity versus resilience. A single PostgreSQL primary is trivially correct but a single point of failure. A fifty-node eventually-consistent Cassandra ring is fault-tolerant and horizontally scalable but requires the application to reason about read-repair, tombstones, and tunable consistency. The architect's job is to draw the boundary in the right place: keep the strongly-consistent core small (accounts, inventory, configuration), and push the rest into eventually-consistent, partition-tolerant subsystems where eventual convergence is acceptable. Netflix does exactly this — billing and playback-entitlement checks go through strongly-consistent services, while watch-history and recommendation features ride on Cassandra's eventual model. Getting that boundary right is what separates a distributed system that scales from one that just runs on multiple machines.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C[Client] -->|request| N1[Node A]
    C -->|request| N2[Node B]
    C -->|request| N3[Node C]
    N1 <-. replicated state .-> N2
    N2 <-. replicated state .-> N3
    N1 <-. replicated state .-> N3
    N1 -- "✗ partition" --> N3
    N1 -->|quorum ack| C
    style partition stroke-dasharray: 5 5,stroke:red,stroke-width:2px
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
           +---------+      +---------+      +---------+
   client  |  Node A | <--> |  Node B | <--> |  Node C |
   -------> | leader  |      | follower|      | follower|
           +----+----+      +---------+      +----+----+
                |                                |
                |  X  NETWORK PARTITION  X       |
                +---------- - - - - -- -----------+
                       (messages dropped / delayed)

   possible states for any node:
     alive  |  slow  |  crashed  |  partitioned   <-- indistinguishable!
```

### Walkthrough
1. Client sends a write to the cluster; it lands on Node A, the elected leader.
2. Node A fans the write out to B and C and waits for a quorum of acknowledgements.
3. A network partition severs A↔C; A still gets B's ack and commits the write.
4. C is alive but unreachable — from A's vantage point C is indistinguishable from crashed.
5. A future read routed to C may return stale data until the partition heals and replication catches up.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Distributed counter mock: three nodes coordinate via message passing.
# Demonstrates how a partition forces a CP vs AP choice.
import random, threading, time

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.value = 0
        self.partitioned_from = set()   # peers we cannot reach
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def increment(self, delta=1):
        with self.lock:
            self.value += delta

    def read(self):
        with self.lock:
            return self.value

class Cluster:
    def __init__(self, names):
        self.nodes = {n: Node(n) for n in names}

    def partition(self, a, b):
        self.nodes[a].partitioned_from.add(b)
        self.nodes[b].partitioned_from.add(a)

    def strong_increment(self, leader, delta=1):     # CP: needs quorum
        peers = [n for n in self.nodes if n != leader
                 and n not in self.nodes[leader].partitioned_from]
        if len(peers) < 1:                            # no quorum
            return False                              # refuse to serve
        self.nodes[leader].increment(delta)
        for p in peers: self.nodes[p].increment(delta)
        return True

    def available_increment(self, leader, delta=1):  # AP: always serve
        self.nodes[leader].increment(delta)
        return True                                   # replicas catch up later

c = Cluster(["A", "B", "C"])
print("start A,B,C =", [c.nodes[n].read() for n in ["A", "B", "C"]])
c.strong_increment("A"); print("after CP write :", [c.nodes[n].read() for n in ["A","B","C"]])
c.partition("A", "C")
ok = c.strong_increment("A"); print("CP write under partition:", ok)
ok = c.available_increment("A"); print("AP write under partition:", ok)
print("final A,B,C =", [c.nodes[n].read() for n in ["A", "B", "C"]])
```

quiz.explanation: A distributed system is a set of autonomous machines that cooperate to deliver a service whose correctness depends on coordination rather than shared memory. The word "only" matters because it rules out the convenient primitives a single-process program relies on: shared variables, mutexes, atomic test-and-set, and a single global clock.

quiz.explanation: Partial failure is the state where some components of a distributed system fail while others continue to operate. On a single machine a crash is binary — either the process is alive or it is dead, and the OS cleans up resources atomically. In a distributed system a node can be alive but unreachable, reachable but slow, slow but functional, or functional but lying (Byzantine).

Google Spanner is CP/EL: it uses TrueTime and Paxos groups to remain linearizable even under partition, and pays a commit-wait latency cost normally.

options: Partial failure is the state where some components of a distributed system fail while others continue to operate.
Cassandra offers multi-datacenter replication with tunable consistency per query, no single point of failure (every node is peers), linear horizontal scalability via…
Because the network may deliver a request once, never, or many times, and the only way to make "at-least-once" delivery safe is to make every operation idempotent so…
Wall clocks drift because quartz oscillators vary with temperature, NTP synchronization is bounded but not exact, and even GPS-locked clocks have residual uncertainty…
quiz.explanation: Wall clocks drift because quartz oscillators vary with temperature, NTP synchronization is bounded but not exact, and even GPS-locked clocks have residual uncertainty (Spanner's TrueTime bounds it to ~7ms but does not eliminate it). If two replicas both stamp a write with time.time() and their clocks disagree by 200ms, last-write-wins resolution will silently pick the wrong winner.
